title: Lady Poverty
hook: Francis marries poverty like a knight marries a lady

segments.voice: Yesterday, the friar: a brother, one of the lesser brothers who chose to be lesser. Your line was lesser brothers. What job nobody wanted did you take? Day one thousand two hundred eleven.

Before he was a saint, Francis wanted to be a knight. His early biographers tell of a cloth merchant's son with fine clothes, generous with his friends, who rode off to war dreaming of glory, and came home changed. He never quite lost the knight's way of talking, though. In the old tales of chivalry, a knight pledged his life to a lady and fought in her colors. Francis found a lady too. His lady was not a person at all. Today's word: poverty.
screen: `A MERCHANT'S SON WHO WANTED GLORY.` → `KNIGHTS PLEDGE THEMSELVES TO A LADY.` → `FRANCIS FINDS HIS LADY.`

segments.voice: Francis's biographers say he spoke of poverty as his lady, even as his bride, the one he'd chosen above every other. Saint Bonaventure writes that he called her by those names. An early allegory goes further, telling of Francis and his brothers climbing a mountain to find Lady Poverty and take her as their companion. It's a love story, not a budget. That's the point. Francis's poverty wasn't stinginess or a grim rule. It was courtship. He went without so his hands would be free for Christ, and for the people Christ loved. Behind it are two lines of Scripture, in the Douay-Rheims. Jesus tells a rich young man: "If thou wilt be perfect, go sell what thou hast, and give to the poor, and thou shalt have treasure in heaven: and come follow me." And Paul writes of Christ: "being rich he became poor, for your sakes." Francis wanted to follow the one who became poor. It cost him. His father, a cloth merchant, brought him before the bishop of Assisi to demand his money back. Francis gave it back, and then, the story says, took off his clothes, laid them at his father's feet, and said that from now on he would call God his father. The bishop covered him with his own cloak. Poor for love, not poor for its own sake. These seven days held two kinds of house. Benedict's family, many houses under one Rule. Oblates, carrying it home. A day in balance. Then Francis on the road: a leper, a gospel taken literally, a brotherhood of the lesser. And now the lady he chose. Two very different ways of giving a life to God, side by side.
screen: `POVERTY: HIS LADY, HIS BRIDE.` · `A LOVE STORY, NOT A BUDGET.` · `BEING RICH, HE BECAME POOR.` · then, large: `POOR FOR LOVE.` · then: `THE WEEK: BENEDICT'S HOUSES, FRANCIS'S ROAD.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: go without one thing. Settle, and breathe. Choose one small thing to do without today. The second coffee. The new purchase. The snack between meals. The background noise. Not as a punishment, and not to prove anything. Hold it the way Francis did: as making room. Then ask who that room is for. Maybe the cost goes to someone who needs it. Maybe the time goes to a person. If you pray, you can offer the empty space to God. The bell holds the time.
Poverty. For Francis, not just having less, but a lady he chose: going without for love of Christ, who became poor. Today's word.
Your line: poor for love. Today, go without that one thing, and give what it frees, money, time or attention, to someone else. Day one thousand two hundred eleven.

howItsDone: Franciscan friars and Poor Clares make a vow of poverty, owning nothing personally, and Franciscan laypeople try to live simply and share with the poor.
